Author: @MrJoshItIs
Content:
I spent 3 weeks in Japan for the 2019 Rugby world cup with a bunch of my boys.  We ate a LOT of ramen, cause it is so good.  It kicked off me getting serious into making it at home.  [meanwhile we have two Michelin starred ramen shops in my hometown of Toronto]

I get how there is the proper recipes, but ramen to me is like tacos or burritos, you can use that canvas and run with it.  That is as lot as you respect what it was intended to be.   I've done duck based ramen with the bone broth done with the carcass and the "chasu" a variant based on the duck breast confit.    I've done similar with thanksgiving turkey.  

I think if you mix poultry and pork bones in your broth they call it something translated to English is "animal style".   I do that often with bones saved in my freezer from breakdowns, etc.   I like chicken feet and pork necks to add a lot of collagen into the broth. 

The broth has to be rich.  The noodles have to be good and you need lots of quality toppings.  There needs to be a balance of salt, savory and umami.  But make your own from what you have.  Come back to the original(s) every so often to check in.

Author: @ikigairamen
Content:
As a ramen chef I should correct some things:
1- in tonkotsu broth you don't cook aromatics for so long, you add to the broth the lasts 30 minutes or 1 hour. Otherwise the sugars from the vegetables caramelizes and turns the broth brown.
2- You should emulsify the broth with a blender to turn it whiter, more creamy but lighter.
3- skinless pork belly is way better than skin on. It turns chewy in ramen and makes hard to break the piece with the teet.
Cheers!

Author: @earthknight60
Content:
Anyone who likes Ramen and who has not watched Tampopo needs to stop whatever they are doing immediately and go watch it.  It's a fantastic many layered Japanese absurdist comedy drama about a restaurant owner learning to make perfect Ramen and save her business.

To give you a taste, this is from right near the beginning of the movie:

Student of ramen eating: [voiceover] One fine day, an old man and I went out for a bite. He's studied noodles for 40 years and said he'd initiate me into the art.

Student of ramen eating: Sensei, broth or noodles first?

Old gentleman: First contemplate the ramen. Carefully observe the entire bowl while savoring the aroma. The jewels of fat twinkling on the surface, the men shoots glistening with fat, the nori darkening with moisture, the scallions floating on top. Above all, the stars of the show: three slices of roast pork, modestly half submerged. Now, then, with the tips of your chopsticks, smooth out the surface and caress the ramen.

Student of ramen eating: What for?

Old gentleman: To express affection. Then point your chopsticks at the roast pork.
Student of ramen eating: Go straight for the pork?

Old gentleman: No, at this stage merely tap it. Nudge it lovingly with the tips. Slowly pick it up and nestle it in the broth to the right. This next step is very important. I want you quietly to apologize to the pork. "Until we meet again."

Author: @rivendoto
Content:
You should've watched The Way of Ramen before doing anything. Yes, it's cool to make your own version, but man, idk about some of the things you've done.

The traditional looked okay, but the broth should've been whiter. I've last watched TWOR like years ago but from what I can remember, after the blanching process, the bones should be boiled with pork fat (like a chunk) in order to let it melt and then emulsify into the broth, making it white. And then, you don't put the aromatic untill the last hour of boiling in order to get the optimal extraction. Then after that, you mix it with the dashi stock.

Knowing that you have the ability to get ingredients somehow easily, I think you should've opted to use Sun noodles. They're a company that makes ramen noodles and even supplies ramen shops according to the shop's preference. I'm not from US but I watched some foods vids and I think they also sell in supermarkets. That fresh noodles would've been better that those dried ones you used (and way, way better than the biggest mistake of using soba for the Guga version) if you don't have the time to make your own noodles.

And you missed out of the aroma oil. It's so simple. You could've just infused scallion, ginger, and garlic in a neutral oil to make a basic one, or fry garlic at different stages of brown to almost black but not burnt, toasted some sesame seed and put it all in a blender with the oil to make a black garlic sesame oil. That would've been delicious.

I don't have that much opinion on the Guga version. I guess you like those things but that's not Tonkotsu ramen for me. I'm not saying I wouldn't eat it. I bet it also tasted great, though I might be turned off with the edamame and the wrong noodle choice.

Hope these helps

Author: @xorngoh7303
Content:
Is that soba noodles? Because to my knowledge as a foodie, only soba noodles have that kind of colour. This is due to the different wheat they use from ramen noodles. Soba is soba and ramen is ramen, they're completely different noodles made with completely different ingredients. Comparing soba and ramen is as good as comparing ramen noodle and spaghetti noodle. They belong to completely different fields and categories of their own. Comparing them is like comparing actual beef meat with bison meat or water buffalo/carabao meat. Or it's like comparing actual pork meat with wild boar meat. They all might look similar with one another, but they're completely different species and categories altogether.
I believe Uncle Roger roasted Jamie Oliver for his "ramen" which used soba noodles. If Guga really used soba noodles for the Guga version, then that bowl of noodles cannot even be called ramen anymore due to the noodles not being ramen noodles in the first place. It should be called hot soba instead. Usually people prefer soba cold and dipped in sauce, but I've had hot soba in Tokyo before during winter. It was awesome. I don't usually eat that much but that night I had omurice with 2 big bowls of hot soba. It was one of the best meals I had in Japan.

Ramen is supposed to be hard and takes days to make properly from start to finish. Don’t insult the hardwork of the history with this.

Author: @adamblanchett6132
Content: Bro... nah. Broth was wrong. Glad you did the pre-boil to clean the scum but you boil it on high rapidly to emulsify the collagen. Time almost doesn't matter. The broth should be thick and milky. Not yellow and watery. Ramen is as much about texture as it is flavor. You have to bring the kombu up to a slow boil. Then remove from the heat. then add the bonito. If you don't get the water to boiling the kombu doesn't extract fully and you get an off flavor. Your tare is fine. You want it super salty as it seasons the whole bowl. Egg is a matter of preference. Skin on "chashu," char sui is Chinese roast pork, is ok but it is better to deskin and add that skin to your broth for extra collagen. Missing the aroma oil. That is such a flavor fail there. Deep frying the enoki is a cool idea but you can just sear it as well. Really glad you torched the chashu. I adds a nice smokiness Interesting seasoning method for your ajitama. I bet the spicy is good. Your other toppings are fine but you missed really hard with that soup.

Author: @nicob5568
Content: Guga man i love you and you make great stuff, but this is not traditional tonkotsu you made. Mistake #1 was not rinsing the bones, the broth shoukd be white not yellow, white means you had too many impurities. Mistake #2 was the chashu pork. Chashu is made by marinating the pork ideally overnight in a marinade mix, then braising, and most importantly COOLING the pork in the fridge then cutting as it retains shape, you did well to char it but you need to cool it first or it can fall apart(also char sui is different from chashu). Mistake #3 is the eggs in the "traditional" as traditional would certainly have them be marinated(not a massive mistake as they can be non marinated but real eggs you use for ramen should be soft yolk that become creamy from marinating). MIstake #4 was not having an aromatic oil in your ramen, very important part of a good ramen. Just make sure to do more research in the future because clearly wherever you had ramen didnt do it well or right if what you made is what they served you
